 Will a power station run a 30 amp RV?
 A power station with a TT-30R outlet can power a 30 amp RV up to the station’s own AC output, not up to the 3,600W the connection is rated for. TT-30 is the 120V, 30A plug and receptacle type on a typical 30 amp RV cord, and 120V × 30A = 3,600W. A connector rating is not available power. The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 has a TT-30R outlet but 2,400W of total AC output, about 20A at 120V (2,400W ÷ 120V, at a power factor of 1). Our van and weekend picks have no TT-30R outlet. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra Plus gives 3,600W in total across its AC outlets, the same figure as the TT-30 rating. EcoFlow’s US page lists up to 30A at its TT-30R outlet and up to 20A at each of its four other AC outlets, all within that 3,600W total. In TheSolarLab’s review (no date shown), the TT-30R outlet shut off first when the total went above 3,600W, even with the extra load on the 20A outlets, so keep the total under that limit when the RV runs from it.
 Among the models we track, the BLUETTI AC200L, Elite 300 and Apex 300, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro and DELTA 3 Ultra Plus, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 and the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus list a TT-30R outlet. Before connecting an RV shore cord, have a qualified RV technician check the station, adapter and RV protection system together, including neutral and ground arrangements and any EMS or GFCI requirements. Do not bypass a protective-device warning or improvise a bonding modification. Before you plug in, switch off the air conditioner and other large loads, then add up what is left. Keep the total within our planning budget of 90% of the station’s continuous output: 2,160W on the C2000 Gen 2 (2,400W × 0.9) and 3,240W on the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus (3,600W × 0.9).
 Count the converter
 When the shore cord is plugged in, the RV’s converter turns 120V into 12V for the lights, the water pump and the fans, and it charges the house battery. A 55A converter such as the WFCO WF-8955 can put out about 790W at 14.4V (55A × 14.4V), and it draws more than that from the station because of conversion losses. If the house battery is low, that load starts as soon as you plug in, and part of the station’s energy goes into the house battery instead of your devices. If you want to disable house-battery charging, have the RV technician identify whether the converter has a dedicated breaker and confirm that the house battery can continue supplying the required DC loads and safety equipment. Do not switch off an unidentified circuit. Otherwise, count the converter in your total. The RV’s 12V loads also pass through two conversions this way, the station’s inverter and the converter, so they use more of the station’s energy than they would from its own 12V port.
 Do not charge the station from the RV while the RV runs from the station. A station plugged into an RV outlet, or into a 12V socket fed by the house battery, would charge itself from its own output through the converter, and each conversion loses energy.
 Air conditioner and microwave
 The rooftop air conditioner is often the largest load in an RV. Dometic’s installation manual lists 12.4A for the compressor and 2.5A for the fan on its 13,500 BTU Brisk II, 14.9A in total. At 115V that is about 1,714VA (14.9A × 115V). We plan with 1,714W, as if the power factor were 1, so actual watts may be lower. At start the compressor can draw 68A for a moment, and Dometic recommends a generator of at least 3.5kW for one unit. That is generator advice, not a rating for a battery station. A station’s continuous output does not show whether it starts this compressor, so check the start-up surge separately with the station maker and the air conditioner maker. A soft-start device can lower the start-up current, but treat it as a condition to confirm with both makers, not as a tested fix. If the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus starts the unit, it runs it at full load for about 1.5 hours by our calculation (3,072Wh × 0.85 ÷ 1,714W), longer while the compressor cycles off. These are examples, not compatibility tests.
 For a microwave, the input watts on the label count, not the cooking watts. Samsung lists 1,580W of input for its 1,000W ME16K3000 and 1,700W for its over-the-range ME19R7041FS. On the Elite 200 V2 , a 1,700W microwave leaves about 640W of our 2,340W planning budget (2,600W × 0.9) for anything else on its AC outlets. Five minutes at 1,700W use about 142Wh at the outlet (1,700W × 5 ÷ 60), about 167Wh of rated capacity at our 85% figure (142Wh ÷ 0.85). More in how many watts a microwave uses and its amps on 12V .

 50 amp RVs
 A 50 amp RV service has two 120V legs of 50A each, a connector rating of up to 12,000W (2 × 120V × 50A). That rating is not what a station supplies. A station feeds a 50 amp RV only up to its own output, and an adapter does not raise it. Ask the RV maker or a qualified RV technician which circuits can run from a station.
 How much power does a van use in a day?

 12V fridge, about 300Wh. Dometic lists 0.98Ah per hour at 12V for its CFX3 35, with 90°F outside and 39°F inside. That is about 282Wh a day by our calculation (0.98Ah × 12V × 24 hours), and we plan with 300Wh.
 LED lights, 150Wh. 30W for 5 hours.
 Roof fan, 160Wh. 20W for 8 hours.

With our 20% allowance on the load energy, the calculated reference size under our assumptions is 862Wh rated (610Wh × 1.2 ÷ 0.85 = 861.2Wh, rounded up). For consistent screening, we apply an 85% delivered-energy assumption to this example. It is lower than our separate 92% DC assumption, but neither validates runtime for a particular station or wiring arrangement.
 The list leaves out phones, a laptop, cooking and heat. A laptop at 60W for 3 hours adds 180Wh. A coffee maker or an induction plate can draw more than 1,000W while it heats, so check its label. The size calculator adds up your own list.

The listed 10A outlet rating exceeds the cooler’s 7.5A rated DC current, but that comparison does not establish spare capacity for additional devices or verify startup. Check shared-output limits and the supplied cable.
 A bigger battery can cover a few cloudy days, but a daily shortfall still empties it. A van that uses 200Wh more than it takes in each day uses up 800Wh of stored energy in 4 days (200Wh × 4).  Can you charge a power station from the alternator?
 From a 12V car socket you can, but slowly. A DC-DC alternator charger wired to the vehicle battery can be several times faster and needs an installation.
 The C1000 Gen 2 supports car recharging with the specified cable, but do not use its 120W car-socket output rating to estimate charging speed. BLUETTI’s US manual (V2.0) lists the car socket input of the Elite 200 V2 at up to 96W from a 12V socket and up to 192W from a 24V socket. EcoFlow’s manual for the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus lists car charging into its solar input at 12V and 8A, about 96W. At 96W, a 4-hour drive adds about 384Wh before charging losses, less than one 610Wh van day.

 How does a power station connect to your RV's 12V system?
 There are two common ways: through the shore cord and the RV’s converter, or through a DC connection to the 12V side under the conditions below. The house battery runs the 12V side, which usually runs the lights, the water pump, the vent fans, the furnace fan and the fridge controls.
 Through the shore cord, the station supplies the RV circuits connected through the shore-power system, within the source and connection limits. That includes the converter that charges the house battery, as the TT-30 section above explains. On the 12V side, the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus has an Anderson port rated 12.6V and 30A, 378W in total shared with its car outlet, by EcoFlow’s US product page, an option for a properly designed connection. A regulated 12V output is not automatically a house-battery charger or a source that may be paralleled with the battery. Do not connect it directly to battery terminals or an energized RV DC bus unless the manufacturers support the arrangement and an RV technician designs the required protection and source isolation. On the C1000 Gen 2 and the Elite 200 V2 , plan the 12V car outlet, listed at 12V and 10A by each maker, for one 12V device such as a fridge, rather than for the RV’s 12V system.
 Use one path at a time. If the shore cord runs from the station, the converter already charges the house battery, so a second connection from the station’s 12V side adds conversion losses, not energy.
 Have a qualified RV technician make any connection to the RV’s wiring, with the right fuse and wire size.
 Can a power station run an RV absorption fridge?
 An absorption fridge can consume substantial battery energy on its electric heating element. If the manufacturer permits propane operation in the intended location and conditions, that mode can reduce electrical demand, while still requiring its specified 12V supply. These fridges, the 2-way and 3-way models in many trailers, cool with heat from a gas flame or an electric element. On 120V, the element heats whenever the fridge cools.
 On propane, the fridge still needs 12V for its controls. Norcold’s manual for its N611 and N811 lists a fault for when the DC voltage is too low to cool on propane. So keep the house battery charged, or supply that 12V from the station only through a connection that meets the conditions in the 12V system section . Our suggestion: while the fridge runs on propane, keep the RV’s CO alarm and LP gas detector working, and follow the fridge maker’s instructions for venting and service. Switch the fridge off propane while you refuel and wherever open flames are not allowed. A 12V compressor fridge such as the CFX3 35 is planned at about 300Wh a day in our van list. Our refrigerator picks and the refrigerator watts guide cover household fridges.
 Solar generator or gas generator for an RV?
 A fuel generator can resume operation after safe refueling, while a station must be recharged. A station runs without fuel or an engine at the campsite. Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide, so safety comes first. Run a generator outdoors only, far from doors, windows and vents, and turn it off and let it cool before you refuel, as the CPSC advises. Our suggestion for a campsite: point the exhaust away from your RV and other rigs, and keep the RV’s CO alarm working. Honda lists 48dB(A) at a quarter load and 57dB(A) at the 1,800W rated load for its EU2200i, without a measuring distance. National Park Service rules prohibit operation above 60dBA at 50ft and can also prohibit unreasonable noise below that level. Site-specific generator hours and other restrictions still apply. One 0.95 gallon tank runs the EU2200i for 3.2 hours at 1,800W, about 5,760Wh of AC output (1,800W × 3.2 hours), more than any of our three picks holds without extra batteries. This compares generator AC energy over one rated-load tank with battery storage capacity. It is not a like-for-like delivered-energy or cost comparison.  EcoFlow DELTA Pro : 1,600W of solar, the same as our full-time pick, a TT-30R outlet, 3,600Wh and 3,600W at 99 lb, and it passes our full-time minimums. It costs $200 more, so it loses the tie on price. It holds 528Wh more and takes extra batteries up to 10,800Wh in total.

 These models did not win under our selection rules on October 28 and 29, 2026, or could not rank because of their stock status that day. Some fit particular rigs better, as their full reviews explain.
 How we chose these picks
 We compared the 32 portable power stations in the PowerSized database, US versions only. It is the list of models we track, not every station sold in the US. A model is eligible when the configuration we price is in stock at the brand’s US store and its price was checked in the last 72 hours. In stock means the configuration can be ordered and ships without a stated future date or a stated wait longer than about a week. Pre-orders, backorders, sold-out and discontinued models, and product pages without a way to order do not count. A model becomes eligible only after its PowerSized review is published. Minimums come first, then one number picks the winner, and a tie goes to the lower price.

 We check outlets on the base unit from the maker’s US spec page or manual. An outlet that needs an accessory does not count. The 1,889W output minimum follows the 1,700W input of the Samsung ME19R7041FS microwave, kept within our 90% planning budget (1,700W ÷ 0.9 = 1,888.9W, rounded up). These rules find the leader on one stated number. They do not test a station with your rig, so the “Closest alternative” and “Skip it if” lines cover other cases. Calculations use unrounded values. Displayed figures are rounded, and minimum capacities are rounded up. The full method is on How we rate .
 Questions buyers ask
 What size solar generator do I need for a 30 amp RV? Size it by your loads, not by the 30 amp plug. A TT-30 connection is rated for 3,600W (120V × 30A), but the station only has to cover what runs at the same time, within its own output. Add the watts of those devices for the output, and watts times hours for the capacity. For our list of a 12V fridge, lights and a fan, three days without sun give a calculated reference size under our assumptions of 2,584Wh rated (610Wh × 3 × 1.2 ÷ 0.85, rounded up), with our 20% allowance and our 85% delivered-energy assumption. It is not a validated minimum for every station and RV.
 How much solar do I need to run a 30 amp RV? Enough to put back what you use each day. With 5 equivalent peak-sun hours, 400W of supported panels deliver about 1,500Wh to the station's solar input (400W × 5 hours × 0.75), before charging losses, about 1,275Wh at your devices at our 85% figure. That is about twice our 610Wh van day. That example is not a budget for sustained rooftop-air-conditioner use. Estimate the air conditioner's energy separately from its operating watts and hours, and verify startup compatibility.
 Can you run an RV off a solar generator? For the 12V system, lights, fans, a fridge and short microwave use, often yes, if the station's output and capacity cover them. A rooftop air conditioner is harder. If the station starts it, a 3,600Wh station runs a 13,500 BTU unit for about 1.8 hours at full load by our calculation, under our illustrative 1,714W operating-load assumption, and the start-up surge has to be checked separately. Count the RV's converter too, which can charge the house battery from the station as soon as you plug in.
 How long will a 2000 watt solar generator run a refrigerator? The 2,000W rating is output, so look at its Wh. A 2,048Wh station gives about 1,741Wh at our 85% figure. A 12V compressor fridge planned at about 300Wh a day, like the Dometic CFX3 35 (about 282Wh a day at 90°F outside by our calculation from Dometic's figure), runs about 5.8 days on that (1,741 ÷ 300), without sun and before any allowance. An absorption fridge on its electric heating element can use far more. Propane mode, where its maker permits it, can reduce that demand and still needs its specified 12V supply.
 What can a 1000W portable power station run? A 1,000W rating tells you what can run at once, not for how long. In a van, it can run a 12V fridge, lights, a fan and phone charging when their total stays within its output and its 12V port's current limit. It does not run an RV microwave that draws 1,580 to 1,700W from the outlet, like the two Samsung models above. How long the rest runs depends on the station's Wh.
 What is the best power system for a camper van? For portable loads with compatible plug-in connections, a power station can avoid a built-in electrical installation. A hardwired roof fan or connection to the RV's DC system still requires the supported arrangement described in the 12V-system section. Under our assumptions, a station with a 12V outlet and panels can cover a 610Wh day of a fridge, lights and a fan like ours. A built-in system with a house battery, a DC-DC charger and a solar controller holds more but needs installation. Our van pick, the C1000 Gen 2 with 600W of solar input, fits the first case. Start from your daily Wh and how you charge between stops.

Best Portable Power Stations for RV Full-Timers (2026) | The Power Station Guide 
 Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. We may earn a commission on qualifying purchases at no extra cost to you.
 Choosing the best portable power station for RV full-time living isn't about buying the biggest battery you can afford — it's about building a system that can replace every watt you use, every day. When your RV is your home, the question stops being "how long will this run my fridge?" and becomes "can this system refill itself by tomorrow afternoon?"
 There's a reason a 2,048Wh pack feels dramatically smaller in daily use than the label suggests. Once you apply a realistic state-of-charge window and account for the gap between rated and usable capacity , a 2kWh system delivers roughly 1.4–1.5kWh of repeatable AC energy per day. For a full-timer, that single number reshapes the entire decision — and most rankings ignore it.
 This guide ranks nine current stations not by headline watt-hours, but by the question a full-timer actually asks: can the system replace yesterday's energy every day? For each pick we weigh daily usable energy, solar and alternator recharge, RV outlet reality, expansion you can still buy, and air-conditioner startup behavior.
 It's written for people whose RV is their home — full-timers, boondockers, and van-lifers who treat shore power as occasional rather than guaranteed. If you're a weekend camper, the general RV guide is a better starting point.
 Quick Picks

 What Makes a Great Power Station for Full-Time RV Living
 Daily usable energy, not the box number. A 2,048Wh station does not give you 2,048Wh of repeatable AC energy. Using an 80% daily state-of-charge window and 85–92% AC conversion efficiency leaves roughly 68–74% of nominal capacity — about 1.4–1.5kWh per day from a 2kWh pack. This is the planning number that matters, and it's covered in depth in the efficiency guide .
 Recharge speed and redundancy. Full-timers replace energy daily, not once per trip. Rooftop solar, 800W alternator charging, campground shore power, and a generator fallback all count. An 800W alternator feed restores roughly 1.6kWh during a two-hour drive — frequently more useful than adding another folding panel. See how it works in the car and alternator charging guide .
 Real RV electrical compatibility. A TT-30 connector is not the same thing as 30-amp service. Several stations here carry a TT-30-shaped port while the inverter delivers far less than 30A at 120V. Check total output first, and treat 12V DC quality and true 120/240V capability as separate features.
 Expansion you can actually buy later. Proprietary battery packs go out of stock — ask anyone still hunting older EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max packs. Prefer current-generation platforms with batteries actively sold today, and read the expandable stations guide before committing to an ecosystem.
 Air-conditioner startup headroom. Running watts are only half the equation. A rooftop A/C compressor draws a startup surge that can trip an inverter that looks fine on paper. Plan for a soft-start device rather than trusting Power Lifting, X-Boost, or a large surge figure alone; see the appliance power guide for the distinction.
 Reliability and support. Firmware errors, accessory failures, and idle draw matter far more when the station is your primary electrical system than when it's an emergency backup. Weight real-world support and idle consumption into the decision, not just the spec sheet.
 #1 — Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 — Best Overall for Most Full-Timers
 The C2000 Gen 2 is the strongest current-generation entry point for serious RV duty. It pairs a genuine 2,048Wh LiFePO4 pack and a 2,400W/4,000W inverter with an 800W alternator charging path, a TT-30 connection, and single-battery expansion to roughly 4.1kWh — all in a 41.7lb chassis, about 20lb lighter than most 3–5kWh systems.
 Key specs 
 2,048Wh LiFePO4, 4,000 cycles to 80% capacity
 2,400W continuous / 4,000W peak AC
 TT-30 RV port — note: total inverter output stays 2,400W, so this is not 30A service
 Expands to about 4.1kWh with one BP2000 Gen 2 battery
 Up to 800W DC/solar input via XT60i; 800W alternator charging; AC + solar simultaneous
 10ms UPS; two 140W USB-C, one 15W USB-C, 12V/10A car socket
 About 9W standby claim; roughly 30dB below 1,000W
 Pros 
 Best everyday balance of weight, alternator throughput, and expansion in the 2kWh class
 TT-30 plus 800W alternator charging covers the two biggest RV pain points
 AC and solar can charge simultaneously
 Cons 
 TT-30 does not mean 30A output — the inverter is still 2,400W total
 One-battery expansion ceiling is lower than BLUETTI's B-series path
 Fan noise becomes noticeable under sustained high load
 Verdict: The most sensible default for a full-timer who wants a real 2kWh system without the weight or cost of a 4kWh flagship. Budget about 1.4–1.5kWh of repeatable AC energy per day from the base pack.
 Perfect for: Full-timers who move regularly and want alternator recharge to matter as much as solar.

 #2 — BLUETTI AC200L — Best 30A RV Output and Mature Expansion
 The AC200L review covers this unit in detail, and the short version is that no other budget-tier station matches its RV-native output. The U.S. model carries a dedicated 30A RV output alongside four 120V AC outlets, and the B-series expansion ecosystem remains the deepest in the class.
 Key specs 
 2,048Wh LiFePO4, 3,000+ cycles to 80% capacity
 2,400W continuous / 3,600W Power Lifting for compatible resistive loads
 Dedicated 30A RV output on the U.S. version
 1,200W max solar input; up to 2,400W AC charging with about 45 minutes to 80%
 Expansion via B230, B210, B300/B300K families — up to 8,192Wh in current U.S. documentation
 Two 100W USB-C ports, USB-A, 12V car output

 Pros 
 A true dedicated 30A RV output, rare at this tier
 Biggest, most mature expansion ecosystem of the budget group
 Very fast AC recharge and a large 1,200W solar input
 Cons 
 Accessory architecture (D40, Charger 1/2, DC hub) is more complex than it needs to be
 Owner reports include occasional accessory and Bluetooth failures
 2,400W continuous won't reliably start a rooftop A/C compressor on its own
 Verdict: The pick for full-timers who want a genuine 30A RV feed and the confidence of an expansion path that has existed for years. Plan on roughly 1.4–1.5kWh of daily AC energy from the base unit.
 Perfect for: Full-timers who park more than they move, and want deep battery expansion rather than maximum alternator throughput.

 #3 — Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus — Best Budget 3,000W Continuous Output
 The Explorer 2000 Plus review explains why this unit still matters: it delivers 3,000W continuous from a 2kWh pack at an entry-tier position, with modular battery expansion that remains commercially available.

 Cons

 Community reports include recurring F2/F6/F7 error codes and reset procedures
 Heavier and bulkier than the C2000 Gen 2
 Verdict: The right choice when you need more raw output than the C2000 Gen 2 or AC200L without jumping in price tier. Budget about 1.4kWh of repeatable daily AC energy from the base pack.
 Perfect for: Full-timers running an induction cooktop, microwave, or other 2,000–3,000W loads on a budget-class system.

 #4 — EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus — Best Fast-Charging Current-Generation Architecture
 The DELTA 3 Max Plus is the newest unit in this roundup, and it shows in the charging numbers: up to 1,600W solar, 800W alternator charging with an adapter, and a 0–80% time as low as 43 minutes using a generator configuration. It's a deliberately modern answer to the daily-energy-replacement problem.
 Key specs 
 2,048Wh LFP, 3,000W continuous / 6,000W surge, X-Boost to about 3,800W
 2–10kWh system expandability; current dedicated bundle with one extra battery reaches 4,096Wh
 Up to 1,600W solar input on current U.S. material
 800W alternator charging compatible — requires a proprietary adapter
 Smart Output Priority via app
 About 25dB at 600W; 3+2 year warranty
 Pros 
 Fastest multi-source recharge profile in the 2kWh class
 Smart Output Priority helps protect critical loads
 Quiet operation under moderate load
 Cons 
 Newer platform with far less long-duration RV owner data than the AC200L or DELTA Pro
 Alternator setup requires an additional adapter
 Exact standalone Amazon listing is still settling in
 Verdict: The strongest choice for a full-timer who wants current-generation charging speed and is comfortable being an early adopter. The older DELTA 2 Max's shrinking battery supply is exactly why buying a current platform matters here.
 Perfect for: Full-timers who recharge heavily from solar and driving, and want the latest efficiency and software.

 #5 — BLUETTI Apex 300 — Best Mid-Range 120/240V Power
 The Apex 300 moves the conversation from "what can I run at 120V" to "what can I run on both legs of an RV panel." Its 3,840W continuous output and native 120/240V architecture put it in a different class from the 2kWh units above.
 Key specs 
 2,764.8Wh LiFePO4, up to 6,000 cycles to 80%
 3,840W continuous / 7,680W Power Lifting for compatible loads
 Native 120V and 240V operation, including simultaneous use
 30A/50A AC and 50A in/out high-current rear interfaces
 Expansion via B300K (to 5,529.6Wh) or B500K (to 7,884.8Wh)
 Up to 4,000W solar via SolarX 4K; Charger 1 (560W) and Charger 2 (1,200W) alternator options
 About 20W idle; not waterproof
 Pros 
 Far more continuous output headroom around RV appliances

 Very large solar input ceiling
 Cons 
 Ecosystem complexity: the 58kWh headline requires multiple stations and many batteries
 Not waterproof — BLUETTI explicitly says keep it dry
 Heavier, fixed-installation character rather than something you move daily
 Verdict: The mid-tier pick for serious RV electrical duty where 3,840W and 240V matter. Budget about 1.9–2.0kWh of repeatable AC energy from the base unit.
 Perfect for: Full-timers integrating a station into the RV electrical system with 30A/50A connections and big solar.

 #6 — EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 — Most Proven Premium Workhorse
 The DELTA Pro 3 is the mature premium choice: 4,096Wh of LFP, 4,000W continuous output, 120/240V support, and an owner base that has already logged real daily use. If the DELTA 3 Max Plus is the new architecture, this is the one with the track record.
 Key specs

 120V and 240V support
 Up to 2,600W solar input; about 1,800W grid charging
 Expands via Smart Extra Battery — current official bundle reaches 8,192Wh
 Generator integration up to 3,200W with Smart Generator 4000
 About 30dB at 2,000W or less; 5-year warranty; about 115lb
 Pros 
 Proven through years of owner use, not just spec-sheet promises
 Quiet operation at moderate loads compared with older EcoFlow flagships
 Large 2,600W solar input and mature expansion
 Cons 
 The 48kWh ecosystem figure requires multiple stations and hardware, not just batteries
 Heavy enough that it belongs mounted or on a dedicated cart
 App and extra-battery visibility complaints appear in owner reports
 Verdict: The default premium pick for a new full-time installation when you can afford the step up. Budget about 2.8–3.0kWh of repeatable AC energy from the base pack.
 Perfect for: Full-timers who want proven premium capacity, 120/240V, and the ability to run induction cooking, refrigeration, and office gear daily.
 Check Price on Amazon 
 #7 — Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus — Best High-Output Dual-Voltage Solar
 The F3800 Plus fixes the two complaints owners leveled at the original F3800: restrictive 240V combinations and a limiting 60V solar input. The Plus adds dual 165V MPPT inputs and far better generator integration, while keeping 6,000W of output from a single unit.
 Key specs 
 3,840Wh LFP, 6,000W continuous; up to 12,000W in paired-system configurations
 120V/240V dual voltage; NEMA L14-30 high-current output; TT-30 RV outlet
 Up to 3,200W solar via two 165V MPPT inputs
 1,800W AC charging; 240V gas-generator charging with the Anker Generator Adapter
 Up to six BP3800 batteries per station — about 26.9kWh
 About 136lb with integrated wheels; 5-year warranty
 Pros 
 Dual 165V MPPT inputs are a major upgrade over the original F3800
 Massive single-unit output with 120/240V and TT-30
 Deep one-station expansion up to roughly 26.9kWh
 Cons 
 Proprietary BP3800 batteries are expensive
 At 136lb, it's rollable, not routinely liftable
 165V inputs demand correct array design — voltage matching matters
 Verdict: The premium pick when you need high output and serious solar throughput in one box. Budget about 2.6–2.8kWh of repeatable AC energy from the base unit.
 Perfect for: Full-timers with large roof arrays, 240V appliances, or a habit of running the RV like a small apartment.

 #8 — Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus — Most Total Output
 The Explorer 5000 Plus is the maximum-output option in this roundup: 5,040Wh of LFP and 7,200W continuous from a single station, with native 120/240V and a huge expansion ceiling. A recent owner ran a sump pump, freezer, refrigerator, and fan for about 20 hours during a derecho before needing a recharge.

 Expansion via Battery Pack 5000 Plus; system scalability marketed up to 60kWh using multiple components

 4,000 cycles to 70%+; about 134.5lb; 5-year warranty
 Pros 
 Highest continuous output of any station here — 7,200W
 Expansion headroom far beyond what a single RV battery bank needs

 Cons 
 The 60kWh figure requires multiple batteries and system hardware
 Very heavy; this is fixed or wheeled, not portable

 Verdict: The choice when output is the constraint, not capacity. Budget about 3.4–3.7kWh of repeatable AC energy from the base pack.
 Perfect for: Full-timers running heavy 120/240V loads — large A/C, induction cooktops, power tools — with expansion planned from day one.

 #9 — Goal Zero Yeti PRO 4000 — Most RV-Native, With Reliability Caveats
 The Yeti PRO 4000 is the most RV-native piece of hardware in this list: a genuine 30A-class TT-30R output matched to its 3,600W inverter, 3,000W of solar input, and U.S.-based support. The caveat is reliability — owner reports describe shutdowns near 20% state of charge, a melted AC charge connection, and multiple replacements.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Q: How much capacity do I actually need for full-time RV living? 
 Start with your daily energy consumption , not a round number. Figure your 24-hour load in watt-hours, then assume you get back roughly 68–74% of a station's nominal capacity as repeatable AC energy. A 2,048Wh pack realistically yields about 1.4–1.5kWh per day. If you consume 3kWh daily, you need a 4kWh-class system or a very strong daily recharge plan.
 Q: Can a portable power station run my rooftop RV air conditioner? 
 Continuous wattage is only half the answer. A rooftop A/C compressor draws a startup surge that can trip an inverter even when the running watts are within rating. Adding an RV soft-start is a safer approach than relying on Power Lifting, X-Boost, or a large surge figure to handle the compressor.
 Q: What's the difference between a TT-30 port and true 30-amp service? 
 The connector shape does not guarantee the output. The Anker C2000 Gen 2 has a TT-30 port but only a 2,400W inverter — roughly 20A at 120V, not 30A. The Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus rates its high-current outlet at 25A max. Always match the inverter's total continuous output to your loads, not the plug shape.
 Q: How do I recharge while driving? 
 Use alternator charging where the station supports it. An 800W alternator feed restores roughly 1.6kWh during a two-hour drive. The Anker C2000 Gen 2 supports it natively; EcoFlow's current systems require an adapter; BLUETTI offers Charger 1/2 accessories. Details are in the car and alternator charging guide .
 Q: Should I add an expansion battery or a second power station? 
 If your current output is already sufficient, an expansion battery is usually the better choice. It adds capacity without the idle draw, cabling, and software complexity of a second inverter. Jackery 5000 Plus owners make this point explicitly: more batteries, not more inverters.
 Q: How much solar do I need to recharge daily? 
 Treat nameplate wattage as an optimistic reference, not a harvest guarantee. A practical estimate divides your daily load by peak sun hours and a 0.75–0.80 real-world factor. Also match your array voltage to the station's input window — high-voltage inputs like the F3800 Plus's 165V MPPT require deliberate array design.
 Q: Are these stations waterproof? 
 Mostly no. The BLUETTI Apex 300 is explicitly not waterproof and must be kept dry. The majority of stations here carry no meaningful weather rating. Protect the unit from rain and high humidity regardless of its output.
 Q: Why does my 2kWh station feel much smaller in real use? 
 Because the label describes nominal capacity, not delivered AC energy. Inverter conversion, battery-management reserves, and a conservative daily depth-of-discharge all reduce what you actually get. The efficiency guide breaks down exactly where the watt-hours go.
 Conclusion
 Full-time RV power is a daily energy-replacement problem, not a peak-wattage contest. The station that wins is the one that can credibly put back what you spent — through solar, alternator, shore power, or generator — day after day, without sending you hunting for a discontinued battery pack in two years.
 The default pick for most full-timers is the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 : a genuine 2kWh system with 800W alternator charging, a TT-30 feed, and simple expansion, at a weight you can actually move. The BLUETTI AC200L remains the choice for a true 30A RV output and the deepest mature expansion ecosystem, while the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 anchors the premium tier for anyone who wants proven 4kWh capacity and dual-voltage capability.
 If you're still sizing your system, start with the full RV guide , then work through how many watt-hours you need , the efficiency guide , and the alternator charging guide before you commit to an ecosystem.

 How to Choose a 2000Wh Power Station

 Solar input. Higher solar input means a faster refill on a sunny day. 1,000-1,200W can refill a 2kWh battery in about 2-3 hours of strong sun; 800W takes closer to 3-4 hours.
 Expansion. If you might need more than 2kWh later, choose a unit with an expansion battery now. Expansion packs are usually tied to one model or family, so you can't mix brands.

 Weight. Every unit here is 41-54 lbs. If you'll carry it often, the Anker C2000 Gen 2 and Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 are the lightest.
 Warranty and cycle rating. Read the fine print: some warranty years require registration or buying from the maker's store, and cycle ratings use different end points (70% or 80%).
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a 2000Wh power station replace a home generator?
 For selected circuits, yes. A 2kWh unit can keep a refrigerator, lights, Wi-Fi, phones and a CPAP running through a typical overnight outage. It can't run central air conditioning, an electric range or a water heater, and it will need recharging (solar, wall power or a generator) to cover multi-day outages. Many households pair a power station for quiet, automatic backup with a generator they run a few hours a day to recharge it. Our power stations vs generators guide compares the two.
 How long until the battery degrades?
 Every unit on this list uses LiFePO4 cells rated for 3,000-6,000 cycles. A cycle is one full discharge; using half the battery counts as half a cycle. At one partial cycle a day, that is many years before the battery reaches its rated end point (70% or 80% of original capacity, depending on the maker). A battery at 80% still works; it just holds less. Lithium cells also age with time, so store the unit at about 50-60% charge when you won't use it for a while, and top it up every few months.
 Can I connect solar panels from a different brand?
 Usually yes, as long as you stay within the power station's input limits. Check two numbers: the maximum input voltage and the maximum input wattage. Measure or calculate your array's open-circuit voltage (panels in series add their voltages) and make sure it stays below the limit, for example 60V on the Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 and the Bluetti Elite 200 V2, or 55V on the AFERIY P280. You may also need an adapter from MC4 to the station's port (XT60, XT90 or Anderson).
 Can I run a 30A RV on a 2000Wh power station?
 You can plug in through a TT-30 outlet, but the power station limits what you can run. At 2,400-2,800W you can run lights, the fridge, the water pump and a microwave in turn, but not the roof air conditioner and the microwave together. A 13,500 BTU RV air conditioner draws well over 1,000W while its compressor runs, so it would drain a 2kWh battery in little more than an hour of compressor time.
 Is 2000Wh enough for a CPAP?
 Yes, with plenty of margin. A CPAP without a heated humidifier draws about 40-60W, so a 2kWh unit covers several nights. Turning off the humidifier and running the CPAP from a DC cable, where the maker offers one, stretches it further. See our CPAP power station guide .
 Conclusion
 For most buyers, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus is the most capable 2kWh unit you can buy right now, with the highest output and a 10kWh expansion path. RV owners should look at the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 for its TT-30 outlet and alternator charging, or the AFERIY P280 for more output, more solar input and a longer warranty at a lower price. If you want one box with nothing to add, the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 has the best like-for-like cycle rating and a TT-30 outlet.
 Whatever you choose, size it to your real loads first: list what must run during an outage, total the watts and the hours, and leave a margin.

 Disclosure · We may earn a commission when you buy through links on this page, at no extra cost to you. As an Amazon Associate, WattRatings earns from qualifying purchases. Commissions never influence scores or verdicts — see how we rate . 
 First, the Uncomfortable Truth About 30A
 A 30A RV shore connection delivers up to 3,600W continuously, for as long as you're plugged in . A 50A connection delivers 12,000W. No portable power station replaces that. The biggest unit we track — the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 at 4,000W output and 4,096Wh of storage — can match a 30A pedestal's power for about an hour at full tilt before the tank is empty.
 Run the numbers on the loads that make an RV feel like an RV:
 Load Typical draw 1 hour of use 
 Rooftop AC (13.5k BTU) ~1,500W running, 3,000W+ start 1,500Wh 
 Electric water heater element ~1,400W 1,400Wh 
 Microwave ~1,000W ~170Wh (10 min) 
 Space heater 1,500W 1,500Wh 
 One afternoon of air conditioning is 4,500–6,000Wh delivered — more than a DELTA Pro 3 holds. So the honest framing for this guide: a power station is not shore power replacement; it's a silent, instant subsystem for everything except climate control and resistive heating. Sized and used that way, the 2kWh class is genuinely useful in an RV. Sized as a generator replacement, any unit will disappoint you.
 What a 2kWh Station Actually Does in an RV
 Here's a realistic overnight off-shore (boondocking) budget, excluding AC and heat. Model: runtime = Wh × 0.85 ÷ (watts × duty). Full assumptions in our methodology .
 Load Spec 24-hr delivered Wh 
 12V compressor fridge 60W at 40% duty 576 
 Lighting 20W × 5 hr 100 
 Phones/tablets (4 charges) 15Wh each 60 
 Laptop 60W × 3 hr 180 
 Water pump, fans, misc ~150Wh 150 
 Coffee maker, 1 pot 950W, ~160Wh 160 
 Total ~1,225Wh 
 That's ~1,440Wh of rated capacity after inverter losses — comfortably inside a 2kWh unit with about 20% margin. The 2kWh class is therefore the correct size for one full day of everything-but-climate , with solar extending it indefinitely. Sanity-check your own fridge in Can It Run: Mini Fridge and build your own line-item budget in the runtime calculator .
 The 2kWh Class, Compared
 Station Wh AC W Surge Solar in lbs 0–80% WattScore

 Anker SOLIX F2000 2,048 2,400 3,600 1,000W 67.2 84 min 85 
 Bluetti Elite 200 v2 2,073 2,600 5,200 1,000W 53.4 70 min 88 
 Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus — best for solar-first setups
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus leads the class on the two specs that matter most for RV use: a 3,000W inverter with 6,000W surge (it will start almost any single appliance you throw at it short of the rooftop AC compressor on a hot day), and 1,400W of solar input — 40% more than the other two. If your roof or ground array is large, this is the unit that can actually use it.
 Who it's for: boondockers building around solar. The 6,000W surge also makes it the safest pick if you're unsure what your RV's startup spikes look like.
 Bluetti Elite 200 v2 — best capacity-per-pound
 The Bluetti Elite 200 v2 carries the most energy in the class (2,073Wh) at the lowest weight (53.4 lbs — 8 to 14 lbs lighter than its rivals) and recharges fastest from the wall (0–80% in 70 minutes). The 2,600W/5,200W inverter covers microwaves, kettles, and induction plates with room to spare.
 Who it's for: RVers who move the station between vehicle and house, or anyone who recharges from pedestals between boondocking stretches — the 70-minute fast charge means a lunch stop at a powered site meaningfully refills it.
 Anker SOLIX F2000 — the value position
 The Anker SOLIX F2000 matches the class on capacity (2,048Wh) but trails on inverter (2,400W/3,600W surge) and is the heaviest at 67.2 lbs. Its 84-minute 0–80% sits between the other two. WattScore 85 reflects competent-everywhere, best-at-nothing.
 Who it's for: buyers who find it meaningfully discounted. At equal prices, the Jackery's surge and solar input or the Bluetti's weight and charge speed win.
 When 4kWh makes sense: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 (4,096Wh, 4,000W, 113.5 lbs, WattScore 92) is the only portable unit that can briefly behave like shore power — it will run a 13.5k BTU rooftop AC, for roughly 2 hours of compressor runtime. As two full days of non-climate loads, it's excellent; as an AC solution, it's a stopgap for one hot evening, not a season.
 Who it's for: full-timers who boondock for multi-day stretches and want genuine two-day autonomy plus emergency-AC capability. At 113.5 lbs, plan a permanent mounting spot — this is installed equipment, not luggage.
 Ports: What Your RV Setup Actually Needs
 A 30A RV outlet (TT-30) on the station lets you feed your RV's existing distribution panel through your shore cord — every onboard outlet and the converter just work. The 2kWh-class units above offer RV-style output either natively or via adapter; confirm the specific model's port sheet before buying a cord.
 12V/10A regulated DC output matters more than it looks: running the fridge on DC instead of through the inverter avoids inversion losses on your single largest 24-hour load.
 High-wattage solar input ports (and their voltage ceilings) decide whether your panel array is usable at all. Check the input voltage range against your panels' series wiring, not just the wattage number.
 USB-C PD 100W ports charge laptops without waking the big inverter — small loads on the AC bus force the inverter to idle-burn watts all day.
 What to Skip
 Skip any plan that includes rooftop AC on battery (unless you're buying the DELTA Pro 3 for two-hour emergencies). The duty cycle of climate control doesn't fit portable storage economics.
 Skip electric water heating and space heating. Resistive heat at 1,400–1,500W devours a 2kWh unit in ~75–90 minutes. Propane exists; use it.
 Skip the sub-1kWh class for RV duty. A 1kWh unit is half a day of the budget above. Fine as a cab-area device charger; wrong as the house battery.
 Skip oversized panel arrays that exceed the input ceiling. 1,600W of panel on a 1,000W input is 600W of wasted purchase.
 Skip daisy-chaining cheap inverter generators "for backup" before you've measured your actual loads — most RVers who do the line-item budget find the 2kWh station plus propane covers everything but summer AC.
 Compare the full port sheets and spec lines for every unit in the station database .
 FAQ
 Can a power station run my RV air conditioner?
 Only the largest units can start and run a 13.5k BTU rooftop AC (~1,500W running, 3,000W+ surge), and even then the math is brutal: a 4,096Wh DELTA Pro 3 delivers roughly 2 hours of compressor runtime. For the 2kWh class, treat AC as out of scope. Soft-start kits lower the surge barrier but do nothing about energy consumption.
 Should I plug my whole RV into the station via the shore cord?
 Yes, if the station offers a TT-30/RV output — it's the cleanest setup because every onboard outlet works normally. One caution: your RV's converter/charger will try to charge the chassis batteries from the station, which can quietly add 100–300W of draw. Switch the converter off when running from the station.
 How much solar do I need to boondock indefinitely?
 Against the ~1,225Wh/day budget above, you need to harvest ~1,450Wh/day (accounting for inverter losses). At a 70% real-world derate and 4 good sun hours, that's about 520W of panel — call it 600W for weather margin. The Explorer 2000 Plus's 1,400W ceiling gives you room to over-panel for cloudy regions.
 Is the 2kWh class too heavy to be "portable"?
 At 53–67 lbs, these are two-hand or wheeled units. In RV use that's mostly irrelevant — the station finds a home near the shore-cord hatch and stays there. If you genuinely need to carry power to a separate campsite regularly, keep a sub-10 lb unit alongside for that job.

 All four use lithium iron phosphate, or LiFePO4/LFP, battery chemistry. That is what I would want in a power station I expected to keep for years and maintain as emergency equipment rather than something I planned to replace after a few hundred charge cycles.
 Best Overall: Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2
 The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 strikes the best balance in this group.
 It stores 2,048Wh, delivers up to 2,400W of normal AC output and handles a 4,000W peak. Yet it weighs only 41.7 pounds, barely more than the Jackery and considerably less than either the EcoFlow or BLUETTI.
 More importantly, Anker did not get the weight down by turning it into a stripped-down battery box. It accepts up to 800W of solar input, provides two high-power USB-C ports capable of up to 140W each, includes a TT-30 outlet and can be expanded with an Anker SOLIX BP2000 Gen 2 battery to roughly 4kWh.
 That combination gives it room to grow beyond basic refrigerator-and-router duty without making you carry a 50-plus-pound unit from day one.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 on Amazon 
 Anker also rates the C2000 Gen 2 for a 10ms UPS switchover. I would still use a traditional UPS for sensitive networking equipment and a NAS rather than replacing one with a giant power station merely because the spec sheet says UPS. But it is useful when the C2000 is sitting between the wall and equipment you want to keep running through an outage.
 The C2000 Gen 2’s biggest limitation relative to the EcoFlow is output. A 2,400W inverter is enough for a huge range of household equipment, but the EcoFlow’s 3,000W inverter gives it noticeably more headroom for high-draw appliances.
 For most people shopping in this size range, though, I think the Anker offers the best compromise.
 Best If You Actually Want to Carry It: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is the lightweight champion here, although calling a 39.5-pound battery lightweight requires some generosity with the English language.
 Still, the difference is substantial. It is almost 14 pounds lighter than the BLUETTI while storing essentially the same amount of energy.
 The Jackery provides 2,042Wh of capacity, 2,200W of continuous AC output and a rated 4,400W surge. It has three AC outlets, USB-C output up to 100W and uses an LFP battery rated by Jackery for 4,000 cycles to at least 70% capacity.
 Check the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 on Amazon 
 There is a tradeoff. The Explorer 2000 v2 accepts a maximum of 400W of solar input. That is half what the Anker accepts and less than half the 1,000W maximum of the EcoFlow and BLUETTI.
 For an overnight outage, that may mean very little. For several days without grid power, it matters quite a bit.
 Suppose you have consumed 1,500Wh overnight and wake up to a sunny morning. A theoretical 1,000W solar array has a much better chance of replacing a large portion of that energy during the useful daylight window than a system limited to 400W. Real solar output will of course be lower than the panels’ nameplate rating much of the time because of clouds, sun angle, temperature and other losses.
 The Jackery therefore makes the most sense to me for someone who wants a self-contained 2kWh battery, expects to recharge primarily from the wall and values portability more than building a larger solar-backed system.
 Most Capable: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus
 The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus is the brute-force option.
 Its battery is still 2,048Wh, virtually identical to the Anker, but EcoFlow pairs it with a 3,000W AC inverter and rates surge output at 6,000W. It also accepts up to 1,000W of photovoltaic input.
 That 3,000W output changes what you can realistically attempt.
 A refrigerator barely notices whether your power station can supply 2,200W or 3,000W. Neither does a router, television or laptop. But high-draw kitchen appliances, power tools, pumps and other larger loads can bring a smaller inverter much closer to its limit.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus on Amazon 
 EcoFlow also gives this model considerably more room to grow. The company supports configurations from the original 2kWh battery up to approximately 10kWh using compatible extra batteries and the appropriate expansion hardware.
 At that point you are moving well beyond the idea of a portable battery sitting next to a refrigerator. You are beginning to assemble a meaningful home-backup system.
 The price you pay for all of that capability is not merely financial. The DELTA 3 Max Plus weighs roughly 48.7 pounds. That is manageable, but it is nine pounds heavier than the Jackery. If you expect the battery to live in one part of the house most of the time, I would not care much. If you expect to carry it up basement stairs regularly, I would care quite a lot.
 EcoFlow rates the unit for less than 10ms UPS switching and provides four standard 120V AC outlets along with USB and high-current DC outputs. It is the machine I would choose from this group if inverter capability and future expansion mattered more than minimum weight.
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2: Strong Hardware, but Watch the Price
 The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 is an interesting machine because several of its headline specifications are excellent.
 It has the largest battery here at 2,073.6Wh, although the difference from 2,048Wh is too small to matter. More importantly, it delivers 2,600W of AC output and accepts as much as 1,000W of solar input.
 Those are serious specifications for outage use.
 Check the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 on Amazon 
 BLUETTI also gives it app control and UPS capability, with a stated switchover within 15ms. Its 1,000W photovoltaic input is particularly attractive if you expect solar charging to be an important part of your backup plan.
 Then we get to the compromises.
 The Elite 200 V2 weighs 53.4 pounds, making it the heaviest of these four. It is also not directly expandable with BLUETTI’s B80, B230 or B300-series expansion batteries. If you eventually decide that 2kWh is not enough, you cannot simply bolt another battery onto the Elite 200 V2 in the way you can expand the Anker or EcoFlow systems.
 That makes the purchase price particularly important.
 Portable power stations are discounted so frequently that I would never rank them purely by MSRP. A $300 sale can change the answer. If the BLUETTI is substantially cheaper than the Anker or EcoFlow when you buy, 2,600W of output and 1,000W of solar input can make it an excellent deal. At similar pricing, I prefer the flexibility of the other two.
 Why 2,042Wh vs. 2,074Wh Barely Matters
 It is very easy to stare at battery-capacity numbers because they provide a nice clean way to rank products.
 In this group, don’t bother.
 The smallest battery is 2,042Wh and the largest is 2,073.6Wh. The difference is only 31.6Wh, or about 1.5%.
 A 100W load would theoretically consume that difference in less than 20 minutes, before accounting for inverter losses and other real-world variables. Differences in efficiency, standby consumption and operating conditions can easily matter as much or more.
 For practical shopping purposes, these are all 2kWh batteries.
 How Long Will a 2kWh Power Station Run a Refrigerator?
 This is one of the most useful applications for a battery in this class, and also one of the hardest to answer with a single number.
 A refrigerator does not normally consume its rated wattage continuously. The compressor cycles on and off, and consumption varies substantially by refrigerator size, age, room temperature, how frequently the doors are opened and whether the appliance is recovering after having been without power.
 If your refrigerator averages 70W over time, a 2,000Wh battery contains enough theoretical energy for roughly 28 hours. At 100W average consumption, the theoretical number falls to around 20 hours.
 You will get less than the simple division suggests because the battery and inverter are not 100% efficient and because you generally do not want to build an emergency plan that assumes every last watt-hour will be available.
 A reasonable way to think about a 2kWh station is that it can often keep an efficient refrigerator operating through an overnight outage while simultaneously handling smaller loads such as networking equipment, phones and some lighting. Actual runtime needs to be measured with your refrigerator rather than taken from somebody else’s marketing chart.
 Output Watts and Battery Watt-Hours Are Different Things
 This causes endless confusion in power-station shopping.
 Watt-hours tell you roughly how much energy the battery stores. Watts tell you how much power the inverter can deliver at one moment.
 The EcoFlow does not run a 100W refrigerator 36% longer than the Jackery merely because its inverter is rated at 3,000W instead of 2,200W. Their batteries are almost the same size.
 The EcoFlow’s larger inverter instead means it can support a heavier collection of simultaneous loads or an individual appliance that demands more power.
 Think of battery capacity as the size of the fuel tank and inverter output as the width of the pipe coming out of it.
 Do You Actually Need 3,000W of Output?
 Probably not if your outage plan consists of a refrigerator, freezer, modem, router, television, laptops, phones and lights.
 Those are relatively modest loads. A 2,200W Jackery already provides plenty of headroom for most combinations of them.
 The higher-output EcoFlow becomes more compelling when you begin adding devices such as microwaves, kettles, coffee makers, induction burners, larger pumps and power tools.
 There is an important catch: a 2kWh battery is still only a 2kWh battery.
 Running a 1,500W space heater from one of these stations may be technically possible. It is also an excellent method for turning a large expensive battery into an empty large expensive battery in a little over an hour.
 High inverter output gives you the ability to run demanding equipment. It does not create more stored energy.
 Solar Input Matters More During a Multi-Day Outage
 For the first few hours without electricity, solar charging barely enters my decision. I want the battery charged before the storm and ready to go.
 Day two is different.
 The Jackery’s 400W maximum solar input is perfectly useful, but the 800W Anker and 1,000W EcoFlow and BLUETTI systems have a much higher ceiling for replenishing a depleted 2kWh battery during limited daylight.
 Do not interpret a 1,000W solar-input specification as a promise that you will actually harvest 1,000W all afternoon. Portable panels live in the real world, where clouds exist, sunlight arrives at imperfect angles and trees have an irritating habit of being located exactly where you need the sun.
 But a higher input ceiling gives you more opportunity to harvest available sunlight when conditions are good.
 This is also where our backup-power strategy begins to extend beyond simply buying a battery. A power station can get you through an outage. A power station with enough generation behind it begins to become a repeatable energy system.
 Expansion Changes the Long-Term Value
 I would think carefully about whether 2kWh is all you will ever want.
 The Anker C2000 Gen 2 can be paired with an expansion battery to reach roughly 4kWh. EcoFlow goes substantially further, supporting DELTA 3 Max Plus configurations up to about 10kWh with compatible expansion batteries and hardware.
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 and BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 are much more self-contained propositions.
 There is nothing inherently wrong with that. If you want a portable 2kWh box, buying an elaborate expandable ecosystem you will never expand accomplishes very little.
 But if this purchase is the first step toward backing up more of the house, expansion becomes one of the most important differences in the table.
 What I Would Buy for Different Uses
 For General Home Backup: Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2
 This is my favorite balance. It is relatively light, has plenty of inverter output, accepts 800W of solar and leaves you an upgrade path to around 4kWh.
 For Moving Between the House, Car and Campsite: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2
 Saving nine or fourteen pounds matters more once you actually start carrying these things. If 2,200W is enough and you do not need a large solar array or expansion battery, the Jackery’s portability is a meaningful advantage.
 For Higher-Demand Appliances or a Growing Backup System: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus
 The 3,000W inverter, 1,000W solar input and expansion path up to approximately 10kWh make this the most capable platform in the group. You pay for that capability in weight and, depending on current pricing, potentially money.
 For a Good Sale: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2
 This may sound faintly complimentary, but it is not meant that way. Power stations are a category where pricing moves dramatically. The Elite 200 V2 gives you 2,600W output and 1,000W solar input. If a promotion puts it materially below the expandable competitors, the value equation can become very favorable very quickly.
 Should You Buy a 2kWh Battery or a Generator?
 If you have not yet decided that a battery is the right answer, I would not start by choosing among these four.
 A battery power station is quiet, can run safely indoors, starts instantly and needs virtually no attention while operating. A combustion generator can keep producing electricity for days as long as you can safely operate it outdoors and keep supplying fuel.
 Those are fundamentally different advantages.
 We have a full comparison in our guide to portable power stations vs. generators for power outages .
 A hybrid system can also make sense: use a battery overnight for quiet indoor power, then use a generator for larger daytime loads and to replenish the battery. We will be digging further into that approach as we expand our home backup-power coverage.
 My Ranking
 If all four cost approximately the same amount, this is how I would rank them:
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 — best overall balance of weight, output, charging and expansion.
 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus — best capability, especially if 3,000W output or major expansion matters.
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 — best portable choice and arguably the better buy than either of the first two for someone who will never need expansion or heavy loads.
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 — excellent output and solar capability, but its weight and lack of expansion make price particularly important.
 I would not treat that ranking as permanent. Check actual prices before buying. If one of these is $400 cheaper than the others during a sale, that is a real specification too.
 The Bigger Question: What Are You Trying to Keep Running?
 Buying a 2kWh power station because 2kWh sounds substantial is backwards.
 Make a list first. Refrigerator. Freezer. Internet. NAS. CPAP. Furnace blower. Sump pump. Television. Lights. Microwave. Whatever actually matters in your house.
 Then look at both starting power and energy consumption.
 That exercise may tell you that a 1kWh battery is plenty. It may tell you that even 2kWh is nowhere near enough. It may also tell you that the best solution is not a larger battery but a generator, solar panels, an expansion battery or some combination of them.
 That is where I want to take this series next. The useful question is no longer simply whether portable power stations work. They do. The useful question is how much backup power your particular house actually needs—and how to build it without buying thousands of dollars of battery that sits unused in a corner.

 The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is our best overall portable power station for a typical 30-amp RV because it combines a 3,584Wh LiFePO4 battery, 3,600W continuous AC output, a native 120V/30A TT-30 outlet, expansion to about 21.5kWh from one power station, wheels and a retractable handle, and a comparatively manageable 77-pound weight.

 What Makes a Portable Power Station Good for an RV? 
 RV use adds requirements that do not matter nearly as much in a normal camping or home-office power station.
 The Battery Must Match Your Daily Energy Requirement 
 Capacity in watt-hours determines how much energy the station stores.
 If your RV consumes:
 1,200Wh per day 
 then a 2,000Wh-class power station has a fundamentally different role from a 4,000Wh-class power station.
 That does not mean the 4kWh model is automatically better.
 If solar and alternator charging replace most of your daily consumption, carrying another 100 pounds of battery may provide little practical benefit.
 Use our RV portable power station sizing guide before selecting a product.
 A Native TT-30 Outlet Is Convenient for 30A RVs 
 A TT-30 outlet gives a conventional 30A RV a more direct shore-power-style connection.
 But the plug shape does not determine the actual available power.
 For example, the BLUETTI AC200L includes a TT-30 connection but its inverter is rated for 2,400W total.
 The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus has a TT-30 output rated at 120V/30A and 3,600W.
 The Anker F3800 Plus also includes a TT-30, but Anker specifies that outlet at 3,000W despite the station having 6,000W of total AC output.
 The lesson is:
 TT-30 present ≠ full 30A shore-service capability 
 Read the exact port limit.
 12V and High-Amp DC Matter in an RV 
 An RV contains many DC loads.
 Converting:
 battery DC → inverter AC → RV converter DC 
 can be less direct than supplying compatible DC equipment from a regulated DC output.
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 includes a 30A Anderson DC output rated at 378W total alongside additional DC connections.
 The BLUETTI AC200L includes a 48V/8A regulated RV output as well as a conventional 12V/10A car socket. BLUETTI also offers its D40 voltage-regulator accessory for RV DC applications.
 Those features can matter more for serious RV use than another USB outlet.
 Solar Input Determines How Quickly You Can Recover Off Grid 
 A larger battery is useful only if you can replenish it.
 Current manufacturer limits among our recommendations range from around:
 1,000W to 3,200W maximum solar input 
 depending on the exact model and configuration.
 Do not treat the maximum input number as expected all-day production.
 Solar output changes with sunlight, shading, panel angle, temperature, array configuration, and the station’s electrical limits.
 Alternator Charging Can Be Critical for RV Travel 
 A motorhome or tow vehicle may spend hours driving between campsites.
 That makes the alternator a potentially valuable charging source.
 EcoFlow currently offers an 800W Alternator Charger compatible with the DELTA Pro 3 when the required cable/adapter arrangement is used. EcoFlow states that the charger can add approximately 1kWh in 1.3 hours under its specified conditions, while also warning users to verify that the vehicle alternator can safely support the load.
 BLUETTI markets an optional 560W alternator-charging solution for the AC200L.
 These are optional charging systems, not justification for connecting arbitrary high-current loads directly to a vehicle electrical system.
 Expansion Matters More for RVs Than for Short Camping Trips 
 Your RV power requirement can grow.
 An initial system might only supply:
 refrigerator;
 electronics;
 lights;
 television;
 fans.
 Later, you may add:
 longer boondocking;
 Starlink;
 more refrigeration;
 air conditioning;
 electric cooking;
 additional travelers.
 A station that accepts expansion batteries can grow without replacing the inverter unit.
 Expansion therefore carries substantial weight in this ranking.

 What is the best portable power station for an RV? 
 For a typical 30A RV, our best overall choice is the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus because it combines 3,584Wh capacity, a 3,600W inverter, native TT-30, major battery expansion, and a comparatively manageable 77-pound chassis.
 For a more advanced off-grid system with strong solar, DC and alternator capabilities, we prefer the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 .
 What is the best portable power station for a 30-amp RV? 
 The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is our strongest direct 30A match because Jackery rates its TT-30 outlet at 120V/30A and its inverter at 3,600W.
 The BLUETTI AC200L is the lighter alternative if your actual loads remain under 2,400W.
 What is the best portable power station for a 50-amp RV? 
 A 50A RV can theoretically access far more power from campground service than any single recommendation here supplies.
 For high-output load-managed use, look first at the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus or EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 because both support 120/240V architectures.
 Do not assume either recreates unrestricted 12kW campground 50A service.
 Is 2,000Wh enough for an RV? 
 It can be.
 A 2kWh station is useful when your RV loads are modest or when daily solar and vehicle charging replace much of the energy used.
 It may be insufficient for extended air conditioning, heavy electric cooking, or multiple days without charging.
 Is 3,600Wh enough for an RV? 
 For many moderate RV energy budgets, 3.5–4kWh is a substantial amount of storage.
 If your RV consumes:
 1,200Wh/day 
 a 3,584Wh rated battery represents roughly three days of headline capacity before losses and reserve.
 If the RV consumes:
 5,000Wh/day 
 the same battery is less than one day’s requirement.
 Which RV power station has the most solar input here? 
 The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus has the largest manufacturer-specified solar-input ceiling among our five main recommendations at up to 3,200W .
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 follows at 2,600W .
 Which is the lightest RV power station in this list? 
 The BLUETTI AC200L is the lightest at approximately 62.4 pounds .
 It also has the smallest base battery among our five recommendations at 2,048Wh.
 Which RV power station is best for alternator charging? 
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 currently has the strongest clearly documented first-party vehicle-charging ecosystem among these picks through EcoFlow’s 800W Alternator Charger.
 BLUETTI offers an optional 560W alternator charger for the AC200L.
 Can I plug my RV directly into one of these power stations? 
 Some have native TT-30 outputs designed for this purpose.
 That still requires you to verify:
 the RV load;
 station output limit;
 grounding behavior;
 converter load;
 RV electrical-management system;
 manufacturer instructions.
 Do not treat physical plug compatibility as complete system compatibility.
 Can these run an RV air conditioner? 
 Some can, depending on the exact air conditioner.
 Continuous output and startup demand must both qualify.
 Runtime then depends on the battery capacity and how long the compressor operates.
 An air conditioner can consume several kilowatt-hours during extended use, so expansion and recharging often become central to the system.
 Do I need a TT-30 outlet? 
 Not necessarily.
 You can power individual RV appliances directly from ordinary AC, USB or DC outputs.
 A TT-30 is especially useful when you want a straightforward physical connection to a 30A RV shore-power inlet.
 Is 240V useful in an RV power station? 
 Only if your actual RV electrical architecture or loads require it.
 Most conventional 30A RVs use 120V.
 Larger 50A RVs use a split-phase service architecture, but a portable power station’s 240V capability does not automatically reproduce full 50A campground service.
 Bottom Line 
 For a typical 30A RV , the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is our best overall portable power station .
 Its combination of:
 3,584Wh battery + 3,600W AC output + native 30A TT-30 + expansion to roughly 21.5kWh + 77-pound chassis 
 creates the strongest balance of RV electrical fit, stored energy, scalability, and transportability.
 Choose the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 when you need a more capable off-grid ecosystem with 4,096Wh of base capacity, 2,600W solar input, high-amp DC, alternator charging, and sophisticated 120/240V options.
 Choose the BLUETTI AC200L when a 2kWh battery is enough and you want TT-30, RV-oriented DC outputs, expansion, strong solar input, and much less base weight.
 Choose the BLUETTI Apex 300 when you want to build a modular RV energy platform rather than simply buy one fixed portable power station.
 Choose the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus when high continuous output and 120/240V capability outweigh the considerable size and weight.
 But the product comes after the requirement.
 The correct decision sequence remains:
 RV loads → connection method → simultaneous watts → startup watts → daily Wh → recharge plan → required capacity → qualified models 
 If you do not yet know those requirements, begin with What Size Portable Power Station Do You Need for an RV? .

Best Portable Power Stations for RV Travel 
 Skip to content 
 Research-backed What we'd buy today 
 Compare portable power stations for RV travel, boondocking, and campsite backup using capacity, output, charging speed, and real-world fit.
 If we were buying a new portable power station for RV travel today, we would start with the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2. It combines a useful 1,024Wh battery, 2,000W continuous AC output, a 24.9-pound carry weight, and very fast wall charging in a size that still belongs in the word “portable.”
 That does not make it the automatic answer for every rig. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus is more flexible if you want battery expansion and unusually strong solar input. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is lighter and straightforward. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 makes a compelling value case while retaining 1,800W output and high solar input.
 This guide explains how we reached those conclusions, what each unit does best, and how to size a power station around the equipment you actually plan to run.
 Our picks at a glance
 What we’d buy 
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 for the strongest all-around mix of output, weight, and recharge speed 
 Best flexible system 
 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus for battery expansion, ports, and up to 1,000W of solar input 
 Best easy carry 
 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at about 23.8 pounds 
 Best value watch 
 BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 when its current price meaningfully undercuts the others 
 Best buying rule 
 Choose from your real wattage, runtime, charging, and storage needs—not the biggest advertised number 
 Editorial note: This is a researched buying comparison, not a claim that Amy and Ryan personally lab-tested every model. We reviewed current manufacturer specifications, independent testing, warranty and support information, and RV-specific tradeoffs. The article is not sponsored, and the product links currently go directly to manufacturer pages without affiliate tracking. Product availability, bundles, and prices change frequently, so confirm them before buying.
